extraction.research_question: Can domain-adapted affective text analysis measure the emotional polarity of UK parliamentary debates over a century, and does that polarity change over time and respond to national economic conditions such as recessions and labor disputes?
extraction.theory: Emotions shape decisions (behavioral economics, prospect theory, regret theory, neuroeconomics). Politicians represent constituents and so echo civilians' emotions in debate, so recessions and labor conflict should make debate more negative (pp.1-2, p.8). Elections raise positivity. Opposition MPs have accountability incentives to decry downturns, while government MPs avoid recognizing social ills, so the opposition is the channel (pp.13-14).
extraction.data: UK House of Commons Hansard, all debates, oral questions and oral answers to written questions, 1909-2013 inclusive (p.2). About 956.8 million tokens, average 9.1 million per year (p.2). Lemmatized vocabulary of 108506 types with frequency 10 or more (p.3). Unit: lemma-PoS pairs for the lexicon; period-level polarity (yearly N=104 in the ARMAX; quarterly and yearly series elsewhere). Economic series, annual: log days lost to strikes, unemployment rate, misery index (unemployment plus inflation), GDP growth, plus a GDP-based recession dummy and election-year dummy. Sources: Dilipad linked parliamentary data (politicalmashup Hansard dumps); code and files on GitHub lrheault/emotion (p.2).
extraction.method: Word vectors: GloVe, 300 dimensions per lemma-PoS pair, symmetric window of 15 tokens (p.3). Seeds: 200 hand-picked English emotion lemmas, 100 positive and 100 negative (p.3). Lexicon: each lemma scored in [-1,1] by summed cosine similarity to positive minus negative seeds (Eq 1, p.4); top and bottom 2000 kept, giving 4200 words. Polarity y_t: lexicon-weighted mean score divided by the count of all lemmas in the period, with a negation flag zeroing words between a negation cue and punctuation (Eqs 2-3, p.5). Stationarity: Dickey-Fuller and KPSS tests, unit root found (pp.8, S1 Appendix Tables A-D). Main model: ARMAX on first differences with recession and election dummies and 1 or 2 lags, maximum likelihood (Eq 5, Table 2, p.9). Group tests: one-sided t-tests on mean differences (Table 3, p.10). Granger causality: pairwise augmented VAR chi-square tests (Table 4, p.13). Cointegration: Johansen rank test; bivariate VECM with 2 lags in levels, orthogonalized impulse response with bootstrap bands (Fig 4, pp.12-13). Long-run effect: dynamic OLS with HAC standard errors (p.12). Long memory: spectral regression of log power on frequency, alpha in 1/f^alpha (p.7).
extraction.identification: No causal design. Recession and election years enter ARMAX as exogenous binary regressors; Granger tests and VECM are time-series association tools. The authors state the cointegrating relation 'should not be interpreted as a causal effect' (p.12). The opposition mechanism is argued from theory and the group-split Granger result, not from an exogenous shock (pp.13-14).
extraction.scope: Population: UK House of Commons debate text, 1909-2013 (one legislature, one country). Era: a century including two world wars, the 1926 general strike, the 1973-75 recession and the 1980s. Cross-domain portability is asserted and only validated on film reviews (p.5).
extraction.measures: Polarity y_t (Eq 3): higher means more positive debate, standardized for figures; scaling irrelevant to the analysis (p.5). Recession: binary, 1 for years with two or more consecutive negative GDP quarters, annual coding where quarterly data missing (p.9). Election: binary, 1 for a general election year (p.9). Labor disputes: natural log of days lost to strikes per year (p.10). Unemployment rate; misery index; GDP growth rate, not per capita (p.10). Government versus opposition polarity, split by party in power (Fig 2, p.8).
key_findings: Polarity rises over 1909-2013: debates become more positive in recent decades (Fig 1, p.6; text pp.5-7). The rise is robust to NRC, OpinionFinder and SentiWordNet lexicons (S1 Fig, p.7) and appears in government and opposition series (Fig 2, p.8). No slope coefficient is reported in the text.

Recession years lower the annual change in polarity: coefficient -0.198 (SE 0.062) in ARMAX Model 1 and -0.165 (SE 0.063) in Model 2, both significant at 95 percent. Autoregressive terms rho1 -0.275 (SE 0.095) and -0.313 (SE 0.098); rho2 -0.145 (SE 0.104). N=104 years (Table 2, p.9).
Election years raise polarity: coefficient 0.187 (SE 0.069) and 0.183 (SE 0.069) in the two ARMAX models (Table 2, p.9). Text says a similar order of magnitude, about 0.19.

Mean-difference t-tests (Table 3, p.10): recession years differ from other years by -0.219 (t=-2.895, p=0.002; 21 recession years against 83 others). Election years differ by 0.202 (t=2.735, p=0.004). War years differ by 0.002 (p=0.511, not significant).

Granger causality (Table 4, p.13): labor disputes Granger-cause polarity (chi2 9.424, df 1, p=0.002) but polarity does not Granger-cause labor disputes (chi2 0.056, p=0.813). Unemployment, misery index and GDP growth show no significant Granger effect in either direction (all p at least 0.12).

Cointegration (Johansen test, S1 Appendix Table F, p.12): fitted long-run relation y_t = -0.06 - 1.39 x_t (Eq 6, p.12), with x_t the labor disputes indicator. The series stay negatively related, more than one standard deviation apart; authors say this is not a causal effect.

Impulse response (Fig 4, p.13; text p.12): a one standard deviation shock to labor disputes produces a negative polarity response converging to about -0.18. Because the series is non-stationary, the shock is persistent until offset by an opposite shock.

Dynamic OLS (Table G, S1 Appendix; text p.12): long-run effect of labor disputes on polarity about -0.9, roughly 0.9 standard deviations of polarity per standard deviation of disputes, significant at the 99.9 percent level with HAC standard errors.

Party split (Table 4 bottom, p.13; S5 Fig; discussion pp.13-14): labor disputes Granger-cause opposition polarity (chi2 8.048, p=0.005) but not government polarity (chi2 0.092, p=0.761). Impulse responses are larger for opposition parties, which the authors read as the mechanism.
Long memory (pp.7-8): quarterly spectral exponent alpha 1.03 (95 percent CI 0.86-1.20), close to pink noise. Yearly alpha 1.71 (CI 1.38-2.04), closer to Brownian noise, so unit-root methods are used.

Seed-usage check (p.7, Google Books Ngram): relative frequency of the 100 positive seed lemmas fell 9 percent from 1909-1918 to 1999-2008, while the 100 negative seeds rose 2 percent. Authors conclude the trend is not an artifact of seed choice.

Validation (p.5, S1 Appendix): the polarity measure alone predicts up to 80 percent of film ratings accurately, and classifiers adding it compare favorably to other sentiment models. Validation is on film reviews, not parliamentary speech.
extraction.limitations: Lexicon approach does not model full sentence structure, so sarcasm, irony and hyperbole are poorly captured (p.5). Negation handled only by a window to punctuation. Validation is on film reviews, not Hansard. Top-ranked lexicon entries include counterintuitive items, e.g. compound scored -1.00 as a negative verb (Table 1, p.4). Economic series are annual, and GDP growth is not per capita (p.10). ARMAX results shown only for simpler specifications; unit-root and cointegration results rest on tests in S1 Appendix. Authors note the unit-root yearly series implies persistent shocks (p.12). Causal reading is not established; no test of mood-to-decision links. Expansion to other corpora is out of scope (p.14).

summary_md: Rheault, Beelen, Cochrane and Hirst build a domain-adapted emotion lexicon for the UK House of Commons (Hansard 1909-2013, about 957 million tokens). They train 300-dimension GloVe vectors on lemma-PoS pairs, score each word by cosine similarity to 100 positive minus 100 negative emotion seeds, and keep the 4,200 most polar words. Period polarity is the lexicon-weighted sum divided by all lemmas, with a negation window to punctuation. Debate grows more positive over the century, and the rise holds under NRC, OpinionFinder and SentiWordNet. Recession years lower annual polarity change (ARMAX -0.198, SE 0.062, N=104 years, pooled over government and opposition, so UNSTRATIFIED). Election years raise it (+0.187). Labor disputes Granger-cause polarity (chi2 9.42, p=.002) but not the reverse. Split by side, the effect runs through the opposition (chi2 8.05, p=.005) and not the government (p=.761). The design is associational, and the authors say the cointegrating relation is not causal. The lexicon is validated only on film reviews, never on parliamentary speech. For Paul's systems the work matters in three places. It is the method source for the opt-in GloVe seed-expansion helper in the legacy press scorer. It qualifies the general-purpose LSD2015 tone intensity that feeds press_value: domain adaptation is argued for, the default intensity is |net|/words (a polarity magnitude, not a charge), and macro-period shifts in tone are not removed. And it shows that negative-emotion language in a legislature follows institutional role (opposition vs government) and economic shocks. That bears on the affective-N slot, which controls for party but not for majority status or period. All three are UNVERIFIED single-agent readings (DE-062).

summary_issues: Overstated relation: the summary calls Rheault the method source for the opt-in GloVe helper, but the helper header cites Rice and Zorn 2018 and its GloVe settings (rank 50, window 5) differ from Rheault's 300 dimensions and window 15. Rheault is a parallel method.

Overstated validation claim: the summary says the lexicon is validated only on film reviews, never on parliamentary speech. The extracted text reports film-review validation and says it is not on Hansard, but S1 Appendix was not extracted, so never cannot be confirmed; use reported validation is on film reviews only.

Overstated causal verb: the summary says the work shows that negative-emotion language follows institutional role and economic shocks. The paper reports annual associations and says the cointegrating relation is not causal, so reports associations is the correct wording.

Figure-only claim: the statement that the rise holds under NRC, OpinionFinder and SentiWordNet rests on S1 Fig, which is not in the extracted text, so it is supported only by the paper's text description on p.7.
gaps_exposed: LSD2015 tone has never been validated against human-coded intensity on congressional press releases. Rheault's own domain lexicon was validated only on film reviews, so neither the general nor the adapted approach has in-domain evidence here.

The default intensity, abs(net/words) via INTENSITY=net_norm, is a polarity magnitude, not a charge. Mixed-valence heated releases score low. No test compares net_norm with lsd_charge against a behaviour criterion.

Tone and affect measures carry no period or date adjustment. Rheault shows chamber-wide tone shifts with recessions and election years and persists (unit root). Whether member press and interview windows are date-balanced is unchecked.

The affective-N slot controls for party but not for majority or minority status, while Rheault finds negativity concentrated in the opposition. No test splits interview negativity by majority status across the 2019-2026 chamber flips.

The opt-in GloVe expansion helper uses stance words as seeds (support, champion, protect), which blends direction toward credit unions with affect. Rheault-style emotion-only seeds would keep tone separate from stance.
flags: Component description drift: components.txt describes affective_n as z(LIWC) + z(LLM), but emit_affective_n.py:39-43 says LIWC was dropped as a component in round-7b (2026-07-11) and kept only as the convergent anchor (r=+.24). The description should be refreshed.

The paper's ARMAX recession and election coefficients are pooled over the government-opposition fault line that the same paper shows matters, so quote them as UNSTRATIFIED. Only the Granger tests are stratified.

The paper suggests studying emotional contagion over parliamentary networks (Coviello ref 63). Any such use in Melange would put influence-style language on network edges. Treat it as an untested idea, not a recommendation, and never on revolving-door edges.
All bearings are a single-agent reading and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).

extraction.research_question: Do U.S. presidential election outcomes (a Republican versus Democratic winner, and Bush versus Kerry or Gore) causally move equity prices, bond yields, oil prices and the dollar?
extraction.theory: Partisan business-cycle models (parties have different preferences over inflation, interest rates, output and capital and labor shares) versus median-voter policy convergence (Downs 1957). The economic voting channel (Fair 1978) implies reverse causation in campaign-period data, which the paper uses to explain why naive time-series estimates differ.
extraction.data: 2004 and 2000 election-night 10- and 30-minute price changes in CME equity and currency futures, CBOT bond futures and NYMEX crude futures; Tradesports Bush contract (2004); Centrebet odds (2000). Daily closes June 2003 to October 2004 for the campaign analysis. Historical 1880-2004 event returns from Schwert (1990), CRSP and Kalinke (2004); pre-election probabilities from press reports and bookmakers. N: 104 ten-minute and 35 thirty-minute S&P observations (2004). Table 2 and historical N not stated; Figure 4 labels 34 elections.
extraction.method: OLS of change in log financial variable on change in re-election probability, 10- and 30-minute first differences, inverse-period weights, White SEs (Scholes-Williams and 60-minute checks similar). Newey-West SEs for daily, 5-day and 20-day campaign regressions. Two-equation structural system with OLS bound. Wald ratio for yields using TIP and IEF funds. Historical event study of returns on a GOP indicator and partisan shock, plus an incumbent-party term.
extraction.identification: Election-night shocks to the market probability of a Bush win are treated as exogenous: a leaked exit poll around 3pm that later reversed, and the 2000 Florida calls. Wald ratios divide the asset response by the probability response. For the campaign period, one further assumption on the correlation of political and economic shocks is needed; OLS is an upper bound if that correlation is non-negative. For 1880-2004 the assumption is that markets respond to election results rather than other news over a longer window.
extraction.scope: U.S. presidential elections only. Intraday natural experiments cover 2000 and 2004; campaign-period daily data cover June 2003 to October 2004; historical event study covers 1880-2004 (Table 3 sample 1928-1996 and 1880-2004). Outcomes reflect trader expectations, not realized policy.
key_findings: 2004 election night (Table 1, p.7): Bush-versus-Kerry effect on log S&P 500 futures is 0.016 (SE 0.004, n=104) at 10-minute differences and 0.020 (SE 0.005, n=35) at 30-minute differences; text says equity prices 1.5 to 2 percent higher under Bush.

Table 1, p.7: Dow 0.014 and Nasdaq 100 0.019 at 10 minutes (both significant at 1 percent); Nasdaq 0.024 at 30 minutes. Dollar 0.004 (not significant) at 10 minutes and 0.005 (5 percent) at 30 minutes.
Table 1, p.7: December 2004 crude oil futures rise by 1.07 dollars (SE 0.35, 1 percent) at 10 minutes and 1.63 (SE 0.59) at 30 minutes; December 2006 contract is negative and insignificant.
Table 1, p.7-8: 2-year note 0.095 (10 percent) and 10-year note 0.108 (5 percent) at 10 minutes; text says 10-year yields 11-12 basis points and 2-year yields 10 basis points higher under Bush.

TIP and IEF Wald estimates, p.8-9: real yields about 16 basis points higher under Bush from the exit-poll experiment and 11 from the second; nominal about 16 and 15, so the authors conclude nominal moves mostly reflect expected real rates, consistent with expansionary fiscal policy.

Exit-poll episode, p.5-6: Bush win probability fell from about 55 to 30 percent with stocks down about one percent, then rebounded to 95 percent as the exit poll was found faulty and stocks rebounded.

Campaign-period daily closes (Table 2, p.10): S&P 0.087 (daily), 0.128 (5-day), 0.243 (20-day); text says the effect is roughly ten times the Table 1 estimate. Oil coefficients turn negative (-7.27 at 5-day, -12.57 at 20-day), read as reverse causation from oil to Bush odds.

Reverse channel, p.11: a 10 percent S&P rise raises Bush re-election probability by 2.3 points (SE 0.8) using daily differences and 3.3 points (SE 1.3) using 5-day differences; authors call these small relative to economic voting literature.

Bush versus Gore 2000 (p.13-14): with a Centrebet prior of about 60 percent for Bush, lower bounds are S&P +1.3 percent, Nasdaq 100 +3.7 percent and dollar +0.6 percent; the second Florida call gives 1.9, 3.0 and 0.7 percent.

Century of elections (Table 3, p.17; Figure 4, p.16): the market-based partisan shock is significant at 1 percent, with coefficients of about 0.025 (SE about 0.008) in the extracted specifications; authors state a 2-3 percent equity rise with a Republican president. Incumbent-party term adds nothing in the joint specification (text: -0.0046, SE 0.0084).

Bond yields (Figure 5, p.18): no reaction to elections from 1920 to 1976; from 1980 a Republican president raised the 10-year yield by about 13 basis points (p=0.15). Regression change in yields = 0.03 + 1.48 Post1980 + dProb x (0.05 + 12.79 Post1980), R-squared 0.23.

Reagan 1980 (p.18): 10-year yield rose 15 basis points when markets priced Reagan at 80 percent. Congressional control tests across margins 0.5 to 0.72 found no significant effect of winning with control (fn 19, p.17).
limitations: Only two close elections with overnight trading (2000 and 2004); the authors trade generality for precision (p.21).
Estimates reflect trader expectations, not actual partisan policy differences; effects are specific to Bush versus Kerry or Gore, not parties (p.21).
Cannot separate output-growth expectations from tax or capital-versus-labor policy channels; no firm welfare conclusions drawn (p.7, p.21).
Assumes traders do not hedge election wealth effects (fn 5, p.4) and that no other news moved markets on election night (fn 7, p.5).
Reverse causation within election night tested only by splitting the sample at 8pm and 10pm (fn 9, p.6); feedback from markets to votes is not fully excluded.
Campaign-period economy effect is only bounded, not identified; it needs an assumed correlation of shocks (p.11-12, fn 14). Instrument search was not completed (fn 13, p.12).
Bond evidence is thin: bond futures closed for three hours and TIP and IEF data are sparse (p.8-9); authors call these data sparser than they would like.
The 2000 Iowa market tracked the popular vote, not the electoral college, so 2000 bounds rest on Centrebet election-morning odds (p.13).

Historical event window is long and identification tenuous (p.14-15); 1964-72 probabilities are imputed from Gallup with sigma 4.9 (fn 16, p.15); partisan shock validity is questionable for 1916 and 2000 (fn 17); candidate quality varies across Republicans (p.17).
Effect of congressional control cannot be tested directly because markets did not track it before 1994 (fn 19, p.17).
Platform complexity prevents attributing effects to specific policies (p.21). Paper is a provisional IZA discussion paper (p.1).

summary_md: Snowberg, Wolfers and Zitzewitz (IZA DP 1996, 2006; later QJE 2007) estimate how U.S. presidential outcomes move asset prices. Their key move is identification: on election nights 2004 and 2000, shocks to the market probability of a Bush win (a faulty afternoon exit poll that cut his odds from about 55 to 30 percent and then reversed; the Florida calls in 2000) are treated as exogenous, and asset changes are divided by probability changes (Wald ratios). In 2004 a Bush win raised S&P futures about 1.5-2 percent (0.016 at 10-minute differences, n=104), 10-year yields 11-12 basis points and December 2004 oil about 1.07 dollars. Over 1880-2004 a market-based partisan surprise (Republican indicator minus pre-election probability) implies 2-3 percent higher equities under a Republican president. The methodological lesson matters most for Paul: a daily campaign-period regression of prices on win probabilities gave equity coefficients about ten times the election-night estimate and flipped the oil sign, because the economy moves the odds (reverse causation) and common news moves both. OLS is only an upper bound if political and economic shocks correlate non-negatively. For Mentat this bears on the sector growth study: SEATS-W regresses weekly Democratic giving share on prior-week changes in 538 expected seats (2022 House, -3.47 pp per seat, one election, EXPLORATORY), and SHIFT uses expected-minus-current control. Lagging the forecast fixes ordering but not common shocks, so SEATS-W is a correlation, not a donor response. The paper also suggests a sharper design: event windows around discrete forecast jumps and a surprise-coded shock. It says nothing about networks, lobbying or ranks.

Text says the Table 2 equity effect is roughly a factor of ten larger than Table 1 (0.016 at 10-min differences, n=104). Authors attribute the gap to bias from reverse causation and common shocks. The OLS upper-bound statement (p.11, fn 14) concerns the reverse regression of the Bush probability on the S&P (2.3 and 3.3 pp per 10 percent rise), and holds if the shock correlation is non-negative, a sufficient condition.

extraction.research_question: Does a U.S. industry's year-over-year economic performance predict how much it spends on federal politics, through campaign contributions and through lobbying? How does expected partisan control of Congress shape both the amount and the partisan direction of that spending?
extraction.theory: Competing accounts: deep pockets (H1, better years mean more spending); distress (H1-alt, bad years mean more lobbying for relief, as in 2008-09 bailouts); access-seeking (H2, contributions shift toward the party expected to hold the majority); stakes (H3, total contributions rise when a chamber is a toss-up); lobbying tracks current power (H4). Majority status is treated as worth access (committee chairs, agenda control), citing Cox and Magar 1999. Section 8 cites Grier, Munger and Roberts 1994 on potential government benefits and collective-action limits.
extraction.data: Five initial sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto (crypto analyzed separately). Unit: sector by year, with sector by chamber by year for RShare. Proposed period 2008-2025, annual; extension to 1998 possible. About 9 elections in sample, six of which flipped a chamber (House 2010, 2018, 2022; Senate 2014, 2020, 2024). Sources: OpenSecrets bulk data, DIME v4.0 (1979-2024), FEC bulk data, OpenSecrets lobbying, LDA.gov API (quarterly LD-2 since 2008), Iowa Electronic Markets, Cook Political Report ratings (1984-present), 538 generic-ballot averages (back to 1996), FRED. N is not stated; the text implies about 18 observations per sector, roughly 90 sector-years (computed here, not stated).
extraction.method: Pooled panel with sector fixed effects, not per-sector regressions. (1) log contributions on prior-year growth, same-year growth, negative-growth dummy, Midterm, Pres, Tossup, trend. (2) RShare by chamber on growth, Shift, RMajNow, Midterm, Pres. (3) log lobbying on lagged log lobbying, growth, Neg, Unified, Midterm, Pres, sample from 2008. Growth is real, z-scored within sector. Robustness: year fixed effects; Shift x RLean; expected seat change. Inference: wild cluster bootstrap by sector; Driscoll-Kraay where year-level terms enter. Forecasts are used only after estimation, to predict 2026.
extraction.identification: No causal claims (Section 7). Prior-year growth is the main test because same-year growth may be caused by the spending and early-year money precedes most growth (Section 4.1). Sector fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences. Year fixed effects give the cleanest growth test but absorb projected control. Projected control rests on about 9 elections; Shift x RLean adds sector-by-year variation. Lobbying uses current control (unified vs divided) because lobbyists work on the sitting Congress.
extraction.scope: Federal campaign contributions and federal lobbying (LDA) only. Five sectors, possibly expanded to every BEA industry matchable to OpenSecrets codes (about 70 BEA industries). Era 2008-2025 proposed, with possible extension to 1998. Life insurance is mainly state-regulated (McCarran-Ferguson), so federal-only scope is an open question (Section 8D). Fairshake outside spending is not candidate contributions.

Projected control is measured as probability of majority, not raw expected seat gains; seat change kept as robustness check.
Prior-year growth is the main test; same-year growth is secondary because it can be caused by the spending itself.
Cook Political Report final ratings (1984-2022) were correct about 94 percent of the time for Lean, 97 percent for Likely, about 100 percent for Solid.
Cox and Magar (1999) estimate House majority status worth about 36,000 dollars per member in corporate and trade PAC receipts around the 1994 switch; cited in the note, not verified.
Only about 9 elections in the sample; six flipped one chamber.
Fairshake super PAC raised roughly 260 million dollars over 2023-24, mostly from a handful of firms and founders; outside spending, not contributions.
OpenSecrets API was discontinued April 15, 2025; bulk data remain free for non-commercial use.

summary_md: Paul's September 24, 2026 design memo to a secondary advisor (Astra) asks whether a sector's year-over-year economic performance predicts its federal campaign giving and lobbying, and how expected partisan control shapes the amount and direction of that money. It reports no estimates. It sets out five hypotheses (deep pockets, distress, access-seeking, stakes, lobbying tracks current power) and three pooled sector fixed-effects models. Model 1 is log contributions on prior- and same-year growth together (a distributed lag), a negative-growth dummy, Midterm/Pres, a Tossup term and a trend. Model 2 is Republican two-party share on Shift = P minus RMajNow. Model 3 is log lobbying with a lagged dependent variable and Unified control. Inference is a wild sector-cluster bootstrap with Driscoll-Kraay errors. The proposed panel is 2008-2025 with five sectors, about 9 elections and 6 chamber flips. The memo is the method source for the Mentat sector growth study, and the Codex ORIGINAL_MODEL_CONTRACT transcribes it. The R build diverges from it. Each growth timing enters its own model (C1/C2/C3) rather than one distributed lag. Totals carry a signed exp_dem control where the memo calls for Tossup. There is no negative-growth dummy, trend or lagged lobbying term. The primary window is 2020-2025 (three elections), not 2008-2025. Results so far are null or fragile: no stable partisan shift (-0.04, p .76), and the lobbying growth lead flips sign under year FE. The memo's leverage worries therefore apply to the build with more force. The only within-cycle access-seeking signal, SEATS-W (-3.47 pp per expected D seat, House 2022), comes from one election and uses expected seats, the measure the memo demoted to a robustness check. All agent readings here are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

extraction.research_question: Do industries spend differently on politics (federal campaign contributions and lobbying) when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow? Does a published industry growth forecast predict subsequent spending, and do expectations about House and Senate control help explain spending?
extraction.theory: Better performance could supply more money for political spending; weak performance or a weak forecast could instead prompt spending to seek favorable policy. The sign of the relationship is to be estimated, not assumed.
extraction.data: Target panel of annual sector-year observations, 2008-2025, for nine sectors where comparable data exist: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto, Credit Arms, Fintech, Property and Casualty insurance, Telecom. Odd years retained; incomplete 2026 excluded. Unit is sector-year; spending in millions of 2025 dollars. Sources: IBISWorld revenue and archived forecasts; Mentat/FEC contributions split by job tier; Melange LDA and LobbyView lobbying; IEM congressional control forecasts; Minneapolis Fed CPI. Final N is not yet fixed: verified contribution years overlap the congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022. Strict annual growth inputs: 53 in the original collection, 86 in the expanded nine-sector grid.
extraction.method: Multiple linear regression by OLS with a separate intercept per sector (sector fixed effects). Contributions: Y_it = a_i + b X_it + c Pres_t + d Midterm_t + e ExpectedDemHouse_t + f ExpectedDemSenate_t + error. Lobbying adds CurrentDemHouse_t and CurrentDemSenate_t. X is prior actual growth, same-year actual growth, or predicted growth (tests C1-C3 and L1-L3). Growth in percentage points. Job-tier extension: pooled model with sector-by-tier baselines and growth x tier terms, Employee as reference. Chamber extension: linear model of Democratic share of contributions. Further extensions: prior and predicted growth together; year indicators in place of national controls; logged spending for positive observations. Simple regression only to illustrate scatterplots.
extraction.identification: No causal identification is claimed. Identifying variation is within-sector over time, after election-cycle and congressional-expectation controls. Predicted growth is taken from the latest IBISWorld report published by December 31 of the prior year, so it precedes the spending year. Congressional expectations are concurrent IEM averages and may not be known before all spending in a year. Results are framed as associations consistent with a response to public forecasts, not knowledge of firms' private expectations.

Sector membership follows workbook rosters (40 company names) and industry proxies: Credit Arms is a proxy for workbook companies, Telecom is analyzed at component level, and Fintech lacks a comparable annual series. summary_md: Paul's own research plan (dated 2026-09-25) for testing whether industries spend more or less on federal politics when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow. It specifies OLS with a separate intercept per sector, six core tests (C1-C3 contributions, L1-L3 lobbying, each with prior actual, same-year actual, or IBISWorld predicted growth), election-cycle dummies and IEM expected-control covariates, plus job-tier and per-chamber Democratic-share extensions. Its strongest contributions are discipline rules: predicted growth must come from a report vintage published before the spending year, missing forecasts stay missing, null results are kept, and independent-row OLS errors are ruled insufficient with nine or fewer sector clusters. It reports no estimates, and its own readiness check says contributions overlap the IEM forecasts only in 2021-2022. The document is the north star of the built sector growth study (Mentat sector_growth_study, in R). The build honours the inference caution with a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector and Holm adjustment, but departs from the plan in three places: log outcomes rather than dollar levels, a retrospective 2023-2026 expected-control series plus 538 robustness filling the IEM gap, and added Tossup and trend terms. Results recorded in the brain (UNVERIFIED, single path): L3 on LobbyView lobbying b 0.242 million 2025 USD per pp (p 0.033, Holm 0.1125) flips to -0.477 under year FE, growth adds no adjusted R2, and the annual partisan SHIFT is -0.04 (p 0.76). So far the plan's question is answered as no stable growth signal, which bears directly on the live giving forecast that still feeds IBISWorld growth into general giving at 50/50.

extraction.research_question: Does prior-year real industry growth predict subsequent organizational political spending (corporate and trade-association PAC contributions to congressional candidates, and reported LDA lobbying expenditure), and do election expectations (probability of chamber control) predict where PAC giving goes across parties, incumbents and committee members? The growth association is the main question; expectations are a separate, exploratory question.
extraction.theory: Three mechanisms, not a predetermined sign: favorable performance can expand capacity; poor performance can raise demand for relief while reducing resources; threatened policy losses can induce spending in either economic state. Majority status has value (Cox and Magar). Committee access drives reallocation (Powell and Grimmer). Regulatory shocks can lower output and raise lobbying at once, producing a negative association without distress-driven behavior.
extraction.data: Not yet assembled; no N estimated. Unit: industry-year. Case analysis uses five sectors; broad panel may use five to ten sectors or all insurance carriers. Proposed common panel 2008-2024 (about 18 annual observations; 2025 only after source audit). Outcomes: FEC committee-to-candidate PAC disbursements (DIME v4.0 covers 1979-2024 public itemized files, excluding CRP/NIMSP-sourced records); LDA LD-2 lobbying, quarterly from 2008. Growth: BEA real value added. Expectations: chamber-control markets (Iowa Electronic Markets, incomplete odd-year coverage) or archived forecasts, about nine elections, six realized chamber flips. Salience: Policy Agendas hearings catalog (listed through 2021) and Unified Agenda editions.
extraction.method: Main model: log S_it = alpha_i + lambda_t + beta g_{i,t-1} + e, with sector and year effects, estimated separately for PAC contributions and lobbying (never summed). Growth g = 100 (V_t / V_{t-1} - 1) on raw real value added. Alternatives: PPML exponential conditional mean if genuine zeros exist; log initial sector size at t-2 as a control; split growth into g+ = max(g,0) and g- = max(-g,0) for asymmetry; dynamic FE only as sensitivity (Bruno bias correction; Arellano-Bond or system GMM not recommended with five to ten sectors). Expectations study: RShare = sector/chamber baseline + coefficient times earlier P + coefficient times current control + limited calendar controls, with a fractional-response sensitivity. Inference: small-sample cluster corrections, restricted wild-cluster bootstrap, cluster leverage, leave-one-sector-out, Driscoll-Kraay only as sensitivity, randomization inference only with a defensible assignment argument.
extraction.identification: Identification rests on within-sector variation in lagged real growth net of sector means and common year shocks. Lagging fixes ordering but does not establish causality; the Bruno correction does not solve endogeneity in current-year growth. Expectations identification comes from election-cycle variation in earlier control probabilities, with roughly nine elections and six realized flips, so the review treats those estimates as exploratory. Chamber-by-year effects absorb chamber-specific probabilities in a pooled panel.
extraction.measures: Spending: inflation-adjusted PAC contributions and lobbying expenditure (logs). Growth: raw percent change in BEA real value added; standardized growth only as secondary presentation. P: earlier probability of Republican chamber control. M: current Republican control. RShare: Republican share of candidate giving (undefined when total partisan giving is zero). Secondary: incumbent share, committee-member share, expected seat change, lagged count of relevant congressional hearings, pending regulatory proceedings (sensitivity).
extraction.scope: Prospective design for US federal politics: corporate and trade-association PAC disbursements to congressional candidates, LDA lobbying, BEA-classified industries, 2008-2024 (2025 if audited). Excludes unregistered advocacy, state politics, and industry-affiliated individual giving, party contributions, super PAC financing and independent expenditures, which are to be analyzed as separate channels.

summary_md: A design review dated 2026-09-24, filed as Paul's research note, of the Astra brief that became the Mentat sector growth study. It estimates nothing. Its core advice: make prior-year real growth the main question and fit log spending on sector and year fixed effects plus lagged raw percent growth (g(t-1)), separately for organizational PAC giving and LDA lobbying, never summed. Treat election expectations as a separate, exploratory study, because more sectors do not create more elections (about 9 elections, 6 chamber flips). It also says three of the brief's specifications do not test their hypotheses: a contraction dummy is not an asymmetric slope (use g+ and g-); Shift = P - M plus current control only reparameterizes P plus M; and a unified-government term cannot separate expected from current control. On data, it says not to fill missing control probabilities with realized results. It says 538 models that use fundraising create a feedback loop, so a polls-only sensitivity is better. It warns that LDA in-house totals already include retained-firm payments and association dues. With five sectors, it says, use the restricted wild-cluster bootstrap and leave-one-sector-out checks. Against the system as built, several points were adopted: raw percent growth, g_pos/g_neg splits, the restricted wild-cluster bootstrap with a few-cluster guard, LOSO/LOYO, the 538 Lite seat forecasts, and lobbying series that are never summed. Others were not. The primary models use dollar levels with national phase and expected-control controls, and year fixed effects and logs are only robustness checks. The giving outcome is Mentat general giving across all recipient types. The 2023/2025 expected control was filled after the fact by Paul's ruling. The later Codex audit vindicated the review's main warning: the L3-LV lobbying slope of +0.352 flipped to -0.477 under sector and year fixed effects (UNSTRATIFIED, 5 sectors, 2008-2023).
